Risk: Facilities are drawn on incomplete or unenforceable documentation, so the bank cannot enforce its rights on default.
Why this matters: If the paperwork behind a loan is incomplete, the bank may not be able to enforce it in court when the borrower stops paying.
Audit objective: Confirm credit documentation is complete, executed and enforceable before drawdown.
What to review:
1. Completeness of the credit file — agreements, security, conditions precedent
2. Execution and legal review of non-standard documentation
3. Conditions precedent satisfied before disbursement
4. Document custody and retrieval
5. Covenant terms recorded in the monitoring system
Procedures:
1. Sample facilities and test the credit file for executed agreements and evidence of conditions precedent.
2. Test that non-standard terms received legal review before execution.
3. Test whether covenants in the agreement were loaded into the monitoring system, and completely.
4. Test document custody by requesting original security documents for a sample.
Red flags:
1. Drawdowns before conditions precedent satisfied
2. Covenants in the agreement absent from monitoring
3. Original documents that cannot be located
4. Non-standard terms agreed without legal review
Evidence to request:
1. Credit files and agreements
2. Disbursement records
3. Covenant monitoring system extract
4. Document custody records
Measures:
1. Files complete
2. CPs satisfied pre-drawdown
3. Covenants loaded to monitoring

Risk: Security is unperfected or valued on stale information, so realisable value on default is far below what is recorded.
Why this matters: Security is what the bank falls back on when a loan goes bad. If it was never registered properly or is worth less than recorded, that fallback is not there.
Audit objective: Confirm collateral is legally perfected and valued on a current, independent basis.
What to review:
1. Legal perfection — registration, charges, priority
2. Valuation frequency by asset class and independence of valuers
3. Loan-to-value monitoring and breach action
4. Insurance over charged assets
5. Release of security and its authorisation
Procedures:
1. Test perfection evidence for a sample of secured exposures, including registration at the relevant registry.
2. Test valuation currency against policy and re-perform loan-to-value calculations.
3. Test valuer independence and panel rotation.
4. Test that insurance over charged assets is current and the bank is noted as interested party.
Red flags:
1. Charges unregistered or registered late
2. Valuations years out of date on volatile asset classes
3. Same valuer used for all exposures to one borrower
4. Insurance lapsed on charged property
Evidence to request:
1. Collateral register and legal files
2. Registry search results
3. Valuation reports
4. Insurance certificates
Measures:
1. Exposures with perfected security
2. Valuations within policy age
3. LTV breaches actioned

Risk: Borrower covenant breaches are not detected, so deterioration is not acted on and the bank loses its intervention rights.
Why this matters: Loan agreements contain promises the borrower must keep. Nobody checking them means the bank misses the early warning that the borrower is in trouble.
Audit objective: Confirm borrower covenants are monitored and breaches escalated and acted upon.
What to review:
1. Completeness of covenants captured from agreements
2. Receipt and review of borrower financial information
3. Timeliness of covenant testing after each reporting date
4. Waiver and amendment authority
5. Link between breach and risk grading or staging
Procedures:
1. Recompute covenants for a sample of borrowers from their submitted financials.
2. Test whether borrower information was received on time and chased when late.
3. Test waivers granted for authorisation at the correct level and for whether pricing or security was adjusted.
4. Test whether breaches fed through to risk grading.
Red flags:
1. Waivers granted routinely to the same borrowers
2. Financial information outstanding for months
3. Covenants recomputed only at year end
4. Breaches with no effect on grading
Evidence to request:
1. Facility agreements
2. Borrower financial submissions
3. Covenant testing records
4. Waiver approvals
Measures:
1. Covenants tested on time
2. Waivers granted
3. Breaches reflected in grading

Risk: Deteriorating exposures are not moved to specialist management early enough, reducing recovery.
Why this matters: The earlier a struggling borrower is handed to specialists, the more money the bank gets back.
Audit objective: Assess whether early warning indicators work and problem exposures are managed by the right people.
What to review:
1. Early warning indicator design, coverage and response
2. Watchlist criteria and transfer to specialist workout
3. Independence of workout from origination
4. Recovery strategies and their execution
5. Provisioning alignment with the workout view
Procedures:
1. Test whether early warning indicators triggered and what happened when they did.
2. Compare the date deterioration was observable in data to the date the exposure was watchlisted.
3. Test that workout management is independent of the originating relationship manager.
4. Compare recovery outcomes to strategies agreed at transfer.
Red flags:
1. Exposures watchlisted only once past due
2. Relationship managers retaining problem exposures
3. Indicators triggering with no recorded response
4. Recovery strategies never revisited
Evidence to request:
1. Early warning reports
2. Watchlist and transfer records
3. Workout files
4. Recovery outcomes
Measures:
1. Time from indicator to watchlist
2. Exposures in workout
3. Recovery rate

Sub-process: Credit Risk Models and Rating Integrity
Risk: Internal ratings and credit models are inaccurate or overridden, understating risk and regulatory capital.
Why this matters: Ratings drive how much the loan costs and how much capital the bank must hold. Inflated ratings make the bank look safer than it is.
Audit objective: Assess the integrity, validation and use of internal credit ratings and models.
What to review:
1. Model development, validation and approval governance
2. Rating override frequency, direction and justification
3. Data quality feeding models
4. Back-testing of predicted against actual default
5. Use test — whether ratings actually drive decisions and pricing
Procedures:
1. Analyse rating overrides by direction and originator; overrides consistently improving ratings warrant testing.
2. Review validation reports and test whether findings were remediated.
3. Back-test rating performance against realised defaults.
4. Test whether ratings genuinely drive pricing and approval, or are produced after the decision.
Red flags:
1. Overrides almost always upward
2. Validation findings open across cycles
3. Models unchanged despite deteriorating performance
4. Ratings assigned after the credit decision
Evidence to request:
1. Model documentation and validation reports
2. Rating and override data
3. Default history
4. Pricing records
Measures:
1. Override rate and direction
2. Validation findings open
3. Back-test accuracy

Risk: Exposure concentrations breach regulatory or internal limits because connected counterparties are not grouped correctly.
Why this matters: Lending too much to one customer, or several linked ones, means a single failure can hurt the whole bank. Regulators cap this for good reason.
Audit objective: Confirm exposures are aggregated correctly and remain within limits.
What to review:
1. Connected counterparty identification and grouping
2. Aggregation across products, entities and geographies
3. Regulatory large exposure limits and internal appetite
4. Sector, geographic and collateral concentration
5. Breach identification and escalation
Procedures:
1. Test the grouping of connected counterparties against ownership and control data.
2. Recompute large exposures against regulatory limits at several dates.
3. Analyse concentration by sector and geography against appetite.
4. Test escalation of breaches and whether limits were raised rather than exposures reduced.
Red flags:
1. Connected borrowers treated as unrelated
2. Exposure aggregation excluding off-balance sheet commitments
3. Limits raised immediately after a breach
4. Concentration reported only at year end
Evidence to request:
1. Exposure data by counterparty and group
2. Ownership and control information
3. Limit framework
4. Breach records
Measures:
1. Exposures over limit
2. Groups correctly aggregated
3. Breach escalations

Sub-process: Customer Due Diligence and Risk Rating
Risk: Customer risk is rated incorrectly at onboarding, so the level of due diligence and monitoring applied is wrong from the start.
Why this matters: How risky a customer is decided at the start determines how closely they are watched forever after. Getting it wrong at onboarding is a mistake that persists.
Audit objective: Confirm customer risk rating drives due diligence and is refreshed as behaviour changes.
What to review:
1. Risk rating methodology and its factors
2. Enhanced due diligence for high-risk customers and PEPs
3. Beneficial ownership identification and verification
4. Periodic review cycles by risk tier
5. Rating overrides and who may make them
Procedures:
1. Sample customers across risk tiers and test that due diligence matches the rating applied.
2. Test beneficial ownership identification for corporate customers, including layered structures.
3. Test rating overrides for approval and rationale.
4. Quantify overdue periodic reviews and test whether high-risk customers continued transacting.
Red flags:
1. Ratings downgraded to avoid enhanced due diligence
2. Beneficial ownership recorded as the immediate holder only
3. Periodic reviews overdue on the highest-risk customers
4. Overrides made by relationship staff
Evidence to request:
1. Customer files and risk ratings
2. Beneficial ownership records
3. Periodic review reports
4. Override logs
Measures:
1. EDD completed for high risk
2. Overdue reviews
3. Ownership verified

Risk: Correspondent and trade finance relationships are used to move illicit funds because the underlying activity is not scrutinised.
Why this matters: Trade finance and correspondent banking move money across borders in ways that are hard to see through, which is exactly why criminals use them.
Audit objective: Assess controls over higher-risk financial crime channels.
What to review:
1. Correspondent bank due diligence and Wolfsberg-style questionnaires
2. Nested and downstream relationship identification
3. Trade document review for dual-use goods and price manipulation
4. Sanctions screening on trade parties, vessels and ports
5. Country and product risk assessment
Procedures:
1. Test correspondent due diligence currency and whether nested relationships were identified.
2. Sample trade transactions and test document review for over- or under-invoicing and dual-use goods.
3. Test vessel and port screening on shipping documents.
4. Test whether high-risk corridors receive additional scrutiny.
Red flags:
1. Correspondent questionnaires years old
2. Nested relationships discovered by the regulator
3. Trade documents reviewed for form only
4. Vessels not screened
Evidence to request:
1. Correspondent due diligence files
2. Trade transaction files and documents
3. Screening records
4. Country risk assessments
Measures:
1. Correspondents with current DD
2. Trade files with substantive review
3. Screening coverage

Risk: Customers are defrauded through account takeover, authorised push payment scams or card fraud, and the bank bears loss and censure.
Why this matters: When customers are defrauded, the bank often has to reimburse them, and regulators judge how well it protected them.
Audit objective: Assess the effectiveness of fraud prevention, detection and customer reimbursement.
What to review:
1. Authentication and step-up controls for payments and account changes
2. Fraud detection rules, machine learning models and their tuning
3. Confirmation of payee and scam warnings
4. Reimbursement decisions and their consistency
5. Mule account detection
Procedures:
1. Analyse fraud losses by type and channel and test whether controls were adjusted after each pattern emerged.
2. Test authentication for high-risk actions such as payee changes and device registration.
3. Review reimbursement decisions for consistency with the regulatory standard.
4. Test mule account detection — accounts receiving and rapidly dispersing funds.
Red flags:
1. Losses rising in a channel with no rule change
2. Reimbursement declined inconsistently
3. Mule accounts identified only after victim reports
4. Step-up authentication bypassable through a channel
Evidence to request:
1. Fraud loss data by type
2. Detection rule configuration
3. Reimbursement decisions
4. Mule account investigations
Measures:
1. Fraud loss rate
2. Detection rate before customer report
3. Reimbursement consistency

Sub-process: Anti-Bribery, Corruption and Tax Evasion Facilitation
Risk: The bank facilitates bribery or tax evasion through its customers or its own conduct, triggering corporate criminal liability.
Why this matters: Companies can be prosecuted for failing to prevent bribery or tax evasion by people acting for them, even if senior management knew nothing.
Audit objective: Assess the adequacy of procedures to prevent facilitation of financial crime by staff and associates.
What to review:
1. Risk assessment for bribery and facilitation of tax evasion
2. Gifts, hospitality and political donation controls
3. Third-party intermediaries and introducer arrangements
4. Training for high-risk roles
5. Investigation and reporting of suspected facilitation
Procedures:
1. Test the bribery and facilitation risk assessment for coverage of the actual business model.
2. Review the gifts and hospitality register for completeness and approval of high-value items.
3. Test due diligence on introducers and intermediaries and the basis of their remuneration.
4. Test training completion for high-risk and client-facing roles.
Red flags:
1. Introducers paid success fees with no due diligence
2. Gifts register with implausibly few entries
3. Risk assessment not covering key jurisdictions
4. Training completion low in front-office roles
Evidence to request:
1. Risk assessments
2. Gifts and hospitality register
3. Introducer agreements and payments
4. Training records
Measures:
1. High-risk roles trained
2. Introducers with due diligence
3. Register entries vs. expectation

Risk: Cash and negotiable instruments are misappropriated at branches through teller manipulation or vault control failure.
Why this matters: Branches hold physical cash, and small amounts taken repeatedly add up long before anyone notices.
Audit objective: Assess physical and procedural controls over cash and instruments in branch operations.
What to review:
1. Teller limits, cash-outs and end-of-day balancing
2. Vault dual control and access logging
3. Surprise cash counts and their independence
4. Suspense and difference accounts at branch level
5. Negotiable instrument stock control
Procedures:
1. Perform surprise cash counts at a sample of branches and agree to records.
2. Analyse teller differences by individual — small persistent differences can indicate skimming.
3. Test vault access logs for single-person access events.
4. Review branch suspense accounts for aged items.
Red flags:
1. Recurring small teller differences by the same person
2. Vault accessed by one person
3. Surprise counts announced in advance
4. Suspense items cleared just before a count
Evidence to request:
1. Cash records and teller balancing reports
2. Vault access logs
3. Surprise count records
4. Branch suspense accounts
Measures:
1. Teller difference frequency
2. Surprise counts performed
3. Aged suspense items

Risk: Payments fail, settle late or are duplicated, causing customer loss, liquidity impact and regulatory breach.
Why this matters: When payments fail or duplicate, customers lose money and the bank has to make it good, on top of the regulatory attention.
Audit objective: Assess controls over payment processing, settlement and exception handling.
What to review:
1. Straight-through processing rates and manual repair volumes
2. Cut-off times, settlement finality and liquidity management
3. Duplicate and erroneous payment detection and recovery
4. Payment scheme rules compliance
5. Resilience of payment channels and contingency arrangements
Procedures:
1. Analyse manual repair volumes and who performs them; manual intervention is where error and fraud enter.
2. Test duplicate payment detection and the recovery of identified duplicates.
3. Test compliance with scheme rules on timing and messaging standards.
4. Review payment incidents and test whether root causes were remediated.
Red flags:
1. High manual repair rates in one channel
2. Repairs performed by the same person who inputs
3. Duplicates identified by customers rather than the bank
4. Recurring incidents with the same cause
Evidence to request:
1. Payment processing data
2. Repair and exception logs
3. Incident records
4. Scheme compliance reporting
Measures:
1. STP rate
2. Manual repairs
3. Payment incidents

Risk: Complaints are not identified, investigated fairly or used to detect systemic customer harm.
Why this matters: Complaints are the cheapest early warning a bank gets. Ignoring them turns one customer's problem into a redress bill for thousands.
Audit objective: Assess whether complaint handling is fair, timely and drives correction of root causes.
What to review:
1. Complaint identification — including expressions of dissatisfaction not logged as complaints
2. Investigation quality, timeliness and outcome fairness
3. Root cause analysis and systemic issue identification
4. Redress calculation and delivery
5. Ombudsman referrals and overturn rates
Procedures:
1. Sample closed complaints and reassess whether the outcome was fair on the facts.
2. Test whether complaints are being logged at first point of contact or filtered out.
3. Test whether root causes were identified and remediated, including proactive redress for similarly affected customers.
4. Analyse ombudsman overturn rates as an indicator of internal decision quality.
Red flags:
1. Complaints resolved verbally and never logged
2. High ombudsman overturn rate
3. Redress paid only to those who complained
4. Root cause recorded as "customer misunderstanding"
Evidence to request:
1. Complaint records and case files
2. Ombudsman decisions
3. Root cause analyses
4. Redress calculations
Measures:
1. Complaints per 1,000 customers
2. Ombudsman overturn rate
3. Systemic issues identified

Risk: Products are sold to customers for whom they are unsuitable, or perform differently from what was represented.
Why this matters: Selling a product to someone it was never designed for eventually means paying them back, often years later and with interest.
Audit objective: Assess whether products are designed, targeted and monitored for good customer outcomes.
What to review:
1. Product approval process and target market definition
2. Distribution against the intended target market
3. Fair value assessment and pricing
4. Post-sale monitoring of customer outcomes
5. Vulnerable customer identification and treatment
Procedures:
1. Test sales data against the defined target market and quantify sales outside it.
2. Review the fair value assessment for products with high margin or low usage.
3. Test outcome monitoring — cancellation rates, complaints, claims declined — for signals of poor outcomes.
4. Test identification and treatment of vulnerable customers in the sales process.
Red flags:
1. Products sold well outside the target market
2. Fair value assessments concluding value in every case
3. High early cancellation rates unexplained
4. Vulnerability flags not visible to front-line staff
Evidence to request:
1. Product approval documentation
2. Sales and distribution data
3. Fair value assessments
4. Outcome monitoring reports
Measures:
1. Sales outside target market
2. Early cancellation rate
3. Vulnerable customers identified

Risk: Credit decisions are influenced by relationship pressure or incentive targets, so exceptions to policy become routine rather than exceptional.
Why this matters: If salespeople can push through loans that break the rules, the bank ends up with borrowers who were never going to pay.
Audit objective: Assess whether credit policy exceptions are genuinely exceptional, escalated to the right level, and performing no worse than compliant lending.
What to review:
1. Policy exception rate by product, branch and originator
2. Level at which exceptions are approved
3. Performance of exception loans versus the book
4. Incentive structures for lending staff
5. Override of automated credit scores
Procedures:
1. Extract all loans booked with a policy exception; analyse rate by originator, branch and product against the portfolio average.
2. Test that each exception was approved at the level the policy requires, not one below.
3. Compare arrears and default rates of exception loans to compliant loans of the same vintage.
4. Review the incentive plan for lending staff and test whether volume targets dominate credit quality measures.
5. Investigate cases where an automated score was manually overridden and trace the justification.
Red flags:
1. Exceptions concentrated with a small number of originators
2. Exceptions approved by the originator's immediate manager only
3. Rising exception rate near quarter end
4. Overrides without recorded justification
Evidence to request:
1. Loan origination system extract
2. Credit policy and delegated authority matrix
3. Arrears and default data by vintage
4. Incentive plan documents
Measures:
1. Policy exception rate
2. Default rate: exception vs compliant
3. % exceptions approved at correct level

Risk: Customer due diligence is incomplete or out of date, and transaction monitoring alerts are closed without adequate investigation, exposing the bank to regulatory enforcement.
Why this matters: Banks are legally required to know who their customers are and to report suspicious activity. Getting this wrong brings fines and, sometimes, criminal charges.
Audit objective: Determine whether customer due diligence, screening and transaction monitoring operate as designed and that alerts are investigated to a defensible standard.
What to review:
1. CDD and enhanced due diligence completeness at onboarding
2. Periodic review cycle for existing customers, especially high risk
3. Sanctions and PEP screening coverage and tuning
4. Transaction monitoring alert backlog and closure quality
5. Suspicious activity report timeliness and quality
Procedures:
1. Sample customer files across risk ratings and test CDD completeness against policy, including source of funds for high-risk customers.
2. Quantify overdue periodic reviews by risk rating and test whether relationships continued to transact.
3. Re-perform screening on a sample of customers and counterparties to confirm the system produces the expected hits.
4. Sample closed monitoring alerts and reassess whether the closure rationale is supportable; measure closure rate by analyst.
5. Test elapsed time from alert to suspicious activity report filing against the regulatory deadline.
Red flags:
1. A single analyst closing far more alerts than peers
2. Alerts closed with template narratives
3. Screening rules relaxed after a volume spike
4. High-risk customers overdue for review still transacting
Evidence to request:
1. Customer files and CDD records
2. Alert management system extract
3. Screening system configuration and tuning records
4. SAR register and regulator correspondence
Measures:
1. Overdue periodic reviews
2. Alert closure rate by analyst
3. Days from alert to SAR filing

Risk: Claims are settled for more than the policy requires because coverage is not properly applied, subrogation is not pursued and reserves anchor the settlement.
Why this matters: Every extra pound paid on a claim beyond what the policy requires is profit gone, and it happens quietly across thousands of claims.
Audit objective: Quantify claims leakage and identify where in the handling process value is lost.
What to review:
1. Coverage verification before settlement
2. Reserve setting discipline and reserve movement patterns
3. Subrogation and recovery identification
4. Use of preferred suppliers and negotiated rates
5. Settlement authority adherence
Procedures:
1. Re-review a sample of closed claims against policy wording and quantify amounts paid above entitlement.
2. Analyse reserve movements: claims settled at or near the initial reserve may indicate anchoring rather than assessment.
3. Identify closed claims with third-party liability indicators and test whether subrogation was pursued.
4. Compare settlement values by handler and by supplier for similar claim types.
Red flags:
1. Settlements clustered just below authority limits
2. Claims closed with no subrogation review
3. A handler consistently settling above peer averages
4. Repeat claimants across policies
Evidence to request:
1. Claims system extract with reserve history
2. Policy wordings
3. Supplier panel agreements
4. Subrogation recovery records
Measures:
1. Leakage as % of claims paid
2. Subrogation recovery rate
3. Average settlement by handler

Risk: Business is written through intermediaries who are not authorised, whose commissions are calculated incorrectly, or who mis-sell products to unsuitable customers.
Why this matters: Brokers and agents sell using the insurer's name, so whatever they do wrong lands on the insurer's desk.
Audit objective: Confirm intermediaries are properly appointed and monitored, and that commission and conduct risks are controlled.
What to review:
1. Intermediary appointment, licensing and vetting
2. Commission calculation and payment accuracy
3. Product suitability and sales conduct monitoring
4. Premium collection and client money handling by intermediaries
5. Complaint and cancellation patterns by intermediary
Procedures:
1. Reconcile intermediaries paid commission to the approved and licensed intermediary register.
2. Recompute commission for a sample of policies against the agency agreement and test clawback on early cancellation.
3. Analyse lapse, cancellation and complaint rates by intermediary and investigate the outlier tail.
4. Test premium remittance timeliness against the agency agreement and quantify amounts held beyond terms.
Red flags:
1. Commission paid to intermediaries with lapsed licences
2. High early-cancellation rates concentrated with one agent
3. Premium remitted late or netted against commission
4. Policies written for customers outside the target market
Evidence to request:
1. Intermediary register and agency agreements
2. Commission payment records
3. Policy lapse and complaint data
4. Premium remittance records
Measures:
1. Early cancellation rate by intermediary
2. Commission error rate
3. Days to remit premium

Risk: Actual production yield falls below standard and the loss is absorbed in variances rather than investigated, masking equipment, material or process failure.
Why this matters: Material that goes in but does not come out as product is money lost. If it is buried in general variances, nobody fixes the cause.
Audit objective: Evaluate whether yield and scrap losses are measured accurately at the line level and driven down through root-cause action.
What to review:
1. Yield and scrap reporting accuracy at each production stage
2. Rework classification and cost capture
3. Root-cause analysis on repeat losses
4. Machine downtime capture and maintenance linkage
5. Bill of materials accuracy versus actual consumption
Procedures:
1. Reconcile material issued to output produced plus scrap for a sample of production orders; investigate unexplained gaps.
2. Compare reported yield by line and shift; test whether the reporting is system-generated or manually entered.
3. Trace repeat scrap causes through to a corrective action with a verified closure.
4. Compare bill of materials quantities to actual consumption for high-volume products.
Red flags:
1. Yield reported identically period after period
2. Scrap recorded in bulk at month end
3. Rework not distinguished from first-pass output
4. Downtime attributed to a generic category
Evidence to request:
1. Production order records
2. Scrap and rework logs
3. Machine downtime data
4. Bills of materials
Measures:
1. First-pass yield %
2. Scrap as % of material issued
3. Overall equipment effectiveness

Risk: Safety incidents are under-reported and environmental permit conditions are breached, exposing the company to enforcement, shutdown and reputational damage.
Why this matters: Safety and environmental breaches can shut a plant down, and they injure people. This is not a financial risk first.
Audit objective: Assess whether safety and environmental obligations are identified, monitored and actually met at plant level.
What to review:
1. Permit inventory and condition tracking
2. Incident and near-miss reporting culture
3. Corrective action closure after incidents
4. Emissions, effluent and waste monitoring and reporting
5. Contractor safety management on site
Procedures:
1. Build an inventory of environmental permits and test compliance with each material condition, including monitoring and reporting deadlines.
2. Compare reported incident rates across plants; a plant with an implausibly low rate warrants interview-based testing.
3. Trace a sample of incidents to root-cause analysis and verify the corrective action was implemented, not just recorded.
4. Test contractor induction, permit-to-work and competency records for work performed on site.
Red flags:
1. Near-miss reporting falling while incidents hold steady
2. Corrective actions closed with no evidence
3. Monitoring results clustered just inside the permit limit
4. Contractors working without a permit to work
Evidence to request:
1. Permit register and regulator correspondence
2. Incident management system
3. Monitoring and emissions data
4. Contractor induction and permit-to-work records
Measures:
1. Total recordable incident rate
2. Near-miss to incident ratio
3. % permit conditions evidenced
4. Corrective actions overdue

Risk: Store staff generate refunds, voids or discounts against genuine sales and remove the cash, or apply staff discounts to customer transactions.
Why this matters: Tills are where cash and staff meet thousands of times a day, and a refund against a real sale is the easiest way to take money.
Audit objective: Identify cash losses arising from transaction manipulation at the point of sale and test whether monitoring detects them.
What to review:
1. Refund, void and no-sale authorisation at the till
2. Refunds without an original receipt or card match
3. Staff discount usage patterns
4. Till variance investigation thresholds
5. CCTV coverage over till points
Procedures:
1. Analyse refunds by cashier per hundred transactions and rank stores and operators; select the outlier tail for CCTV review.
2. Test refunds processed to a different payment method than the original sale.
3. Match staff discount transactions to employee purchase records and test for use on non-employee sales.
4. Test whether till variances below the investigation threshold accumulate to a material amount by operator.
Red flags:
1. Refunds concentrated in the operator's own shift with no customer present on CCTV
2. Repeated small variances just under the threshold
3. Voids immediately after a cash sale
4. Discount cards used at multiple stores
Evidence to request:
1. Point-of-sale transaction log
2. Till variance reports
3. Employee discount card register
4. CCTV footage
Measures:
1. Refunds per 100 transactions by operator
2. Till variance per store
3. Voids as % of sales

Risk: Suppliers under-deliver, deliver late or invoice outside agreed terms, and the store network absorbs the loss because claims are never raised.
Why this matters: If suppliers under-deliver or overcharge and nobody claims it back, the loss is simply absorbed store by store.
Audit objective: Confirm that goods received match what was ordered and invoiced, and that supplier non-compliance is claimed and recovered.
What to review:
1. Three-way match discipline between order, receipt and invoice
2. Short and damaged delivery claim process
3. On-time in-full performance by supplier
4. Price differences between contract and invoice
5. Deduction and chargeback recovery
Procedures:
1. Quantify receipts posted without a purchase order and invoices paid without a matched receipt.
2. Re-price a sample of invoices against contracted terms and quantify overcharges.
3. Analyse on-time in-full performance by supplier and test whether contractual service credits were claimed.
4. Test the ageing of open supplier claims and the recovery rate.
Red flags:
1. Receipts booked in full despite recorded shortages
2. Claims raised but never followed up
3. Price variances always in the supplier's favour
4. A supplier consistently below service level with no credits taken
Evidence to request:
1. Purchase order, receipt and invoice data
2. Supplier contracts and trading terms
3. Claims and deductions register
4. On-time in-full reporting
Measures:
1. Price variance recovered
2. OTIF % by supplier
3. Open claims ageing

Risk: Aircraft are released to service without all required maintenance tasks and airworthiness directives being completed and certified.
Why this matters: An aircraft with incomplete maintenance records cannot legally fly, regardless of whether the work was actually done.
Audit objective: Confirm that maintenance is performed and certified by authorised personnel and that airworthiness records are complete and traceable.
What to review:
1. Airworthiness directive and service bulletin compliance tracking
2. Certifying staff authorisation scope and currency
3. Deferred defect management against the minimum equipment list
4. Parts traceability and approved supply chain
5. Maintenance record retention and integrity
Procedures:
1. Select applicable airworthiness directives and trace each to a completed and certified work package within the required interval.
2. Test that certifying signatures belong to staff whose authorisation covers that aircraft type and task, and was current on the date.
3. Analyse deferred defects for items carried beyond the MEL time limit or repeatedly re-deferred.
4. Trace a sample of fitted parts to release certificates and approved suppliers.
Red flags:
1. Defects repeatedly deferred and re-raised
2. Certification by staff whose authorisation lapsed
3. Parts fitted without an airworthiness release certificate
4. Records completed retrospectively in blocks
Evidence to request:
1. Maintenance information system records
2. Airworthiness directive register
3. Certifying staff authorisation records
4. Parts release certificates
5. Regulator audit findings
Measures:
1. AD compliance rate
2. Deferred defects beyond limit
3. % work packages certified in time

Risk: Ground handling errors damage aircraft, delay departures and generate airline chargebacks that are absorbed rather than investigated.
Why this matters: Damage on the ground grounds aircraft and generates claims from airlines, and it is often discovered by the customer rather than the handler.
Audit objective: Assess control over ramp operations, damage reporting and the recovery or prevention of associated cost.
What to review:
1. Ground support equipment maintenance and operator licensing
2. Aircraft damage reporting and investigation
3. Delay coding accuracy and attribution
4. Load control and weight and balance accuracy
5. Airside driving permits and training currency
Procedures:
1. Reconcile ground damage incidents reported internally to airline claims received; investigate claims with no internal report.
2. Test operator licensing and training currency for a sample of ramp staff and equipment types.
3. Analyse delay codes attributed to handling and test the supporting evidence for a sample.
4. Review load sheet accuracy against actual loading for a sample of flights.
Red flags:
1. Damage discovered by the airline rather than reported by the station
2. Delay codes reassigned after the fact
3. Equipment operated by staff without a current licence
4. Load sheets amended after departure
Evidence to request:
1. Ground damage register and airline claims
2. Training and licensing records
3. Delay reporting data
4. Load sheets and weight and balance records
Measures:
1. Ground damage incidents per 1,000 turns
2. On-time departure %
3. Claims cost per turn

Risk: Front desk staff manipulate reservations, comps and petty cash, and the loss is hidden by the volume of small transactions.
Why this matters: The front desk can give away rooms, discounts and refunds, and each one is money the hotel never sees.
Audit objective: Identify cash and revenue loss at the property and assess whether property-level monitoring detects it.
What to review:
1. Comp, discount and rate-override authority at the front desk
2. Room moves and reservation cancellations after check-in
3. Petty cash and float custody
4. Paid-out and refund transactions
5. Night audit independence
Procedures:
1. Analyse comps, rate overrides and zero-rate stays by agent and shift; select the outlier tail for evidence of authorisation.
2. Test reservations cancelled after the guest checked in, which can conceal a cash sale.
3. Count floats unannounced at a sample of properties and agree to the recorded balance.
4. Test paid-outs and refunds for supporting documentation and guest signature.
5. Confirm the night auditor is not the same person who operated the desk during the shift audited.
Red flags:
1. Comps concentrated on one agent or shift
2. Repeated room moves to lower rate codes
3. Floats counted only by their own custodian
4. Guest folios adjusted after checkout
Evidence to request:
1. Property management system transaction log
2. Night audit packs
3. Petty cash and float records
4. CCTV at the front desk
Measures:
1. Comps as % of room revenue
2. Overrides per agent
3. Float variance per property

Risk: Property managers direct purchasing to connected suppliers at inflated prices, outside the group procurement framework.
Why this matters: When each property buys locally, prices drift upward and personal relationships creep in.
Audit objective: Assess whether property-level purchasing follows the group framework and whether supplier relationships are arm's length.
What to review:
1. Use of contracted group suppliers versus local purchasing
2. Local supplier onboarding and vetting
3. Price benchmarking against group contracts
4. Conflict of interest declarations at property level
5. Splitting of purchases below approval thresholds
Procedures:
1. Quantify spend outside the group contracted supplier list by property and category.
2. Compare unit prices paid locally against the group contract rate for the same items.
3. Match local supplier details against employee records for shared addresses, phone numbers and bank accounts.
4. Test for purchase orders split into amounts just below the approval threshold.
Red flags:
1. A property with unusually high local spend
2. Suppliers created and used only by one property
3. Invoices consistently just below the threshold
4. No competitive quotes on recurring local spend
Evidence to request:
1. Accounts payable spend by property and supplier
2. Group supplier contracts and rates
3. Employee master data
4. Purchase order records
Measures:
1. % spend on contract
2. Price variance to group rate
3. Split-order exceptions

Risk: Pricing and promotion errors are published to the site and honoured at scale before anyone notices, or promotional terms are not met.
Why this matters: An online pricing error is honoured at scale within minutes, before anyone can react.
Audit objective: Assess control over what is published to customers and how quickly errors are detected and corrected.
What to review:
1. Price and promotion change approval before publication
2. Automated checks on price change magnitude
3. Stacking of promotions and discount codes
4. Speed of detection and rollback
5. Advertising and claims compliance
Procedures:
1. Test the approval trail for a sample of price and promotion changes published in the period.
2. Review automated tolerance checks on price changes and test whether they blocked or flagged extreme values.
3. Test whether discount codes can be stacked or reused beyond their intended limit by re-performing a checkout in a test environment.
4. Measure elapsed time from publication of known pricing errors to correction, and quantify orders honoured.
Red flags:
1. Discount codes shared publicly and still active
2. Price changes published outside working hours without approval
3. Repeat incidents with the same root cause
4. No monetary tolerance on automated price feeds
Evidence to request:
1. Content management change log
2. Promotion configuration records
3. Incident log for pricing errors
4. Order data for affected periods
Measures:
1. Pricing incidents per quarter
2. Value honoured on error
3. Mean time to correct

Risk: Personal data is retained longer than permitted, shared with third parties without a lawful basis, or exposed through weak access control.
Why this matters: Customer data is regulated. Keeping it too long or sharing it too widely is a fine, not just a bad look.
Audit objective: Determine whether personal data is held, used and shared in line with privacy obligations and consent.
What to review:
1. Data inventory and lawful basis for each processing purpose
2. Consent capture and withdrawal handling
3. Retention and deletion in practice, not just in policy
4. Third-party data sharing and processor agreements
5. Access to production customer data by staff and vendors
Procedures:
1. Trace a sample of processing purposes to a documented lawful basis and to what customers were actually told.
2. Test deletion by selecting accounts that requested erasure and searching all systems, including backups and analytics, for residual data.
3. Reconcile third parties receiving customer data to signed processor agreements.
4. Review who holds access to production customer data and test whether that access is justified by role.
Red flags:
1. Marketing to customers who withdrew consent
2. Data retained "in case it is useful"
3. Analytics tools receiving identifiable data
4. Vendor access never reviewed after onboarding
Evidence to request:
1. Data inventory and processing records
2. Consent management logs
3. Erasure request records
4. Processor agreements
5. Access listings
Measures:
1. Erasure requests completed in time
2. Systems with retention enforced
3. Vendors with signed agreements

Sub-process: Route to Market and Distributor Performance
Risk: Distributors sell outside their assigned territory, hold stock beyond shelf life, or claim promotional support they did not deliver.
Why this matters: Distributors buying more than they can sell means the sales figures are not real, and the stock comes back.
Audit objective: Assess whether distributor arrangements are performing as contracted and claims are substantiated.
What to review:
1. Territory assignment and cross-territory selling
2. Distributor stock levels and shelf-life exposure
3. Promotional claim substantiation
4. Credit exposure and payment performance
5. Distributor audits performed by the company
Procedures:
1. Analyse sell-in versus sell-out data by distributor to identify stock building beyond normal cover.
2. Sample promotional claims and test for evidence the activity was performed, such as photographs, invoices or third-party verification.
3. Test credit exposure by distributor against approved limits and ageing.
4. Review the company's own distributor audit programme, coverage and follow-up of findings.
Red flags:
1. Distributors with stock cover far above the network average
2. Claims supported by generic or reused evidence
3. Sales spikes before price increases
4. Distributor audits repeatedly deferred
Evidence to request:
1. Distributor sell-in and sell-out data
2. Promotional claim files
3. Credit exposure reports
4. Distributor audit reports
Measures:
1. Stock cover days by distributor
2. % claims with valid evidence
3. Overdue distributor balances

Risk: A product safety failure reaches consumers because quality controls at the plant are bypassed under production pressure.
Why this matters: If a product batch is unsafe, the company must find every unit fast. Poor traceability turns a problem into a crisis.
Audit objective: Assess whether food safety controls operate as designed under real production conditions.
What to review:
1. HACCP plan currency and critical control point monitoring
2. Deviations at critical control points and their disposition
3. Hygiene, pest control and allergen segregation
4. Supplier raw material approval and incoming testing
5. Certification audit findings and closure
Procedures:
1. Test critical control point monitoring records for completeness and for deviations released without a documented disposition decision.
2. Walk the plant during production and compare observed practice to the HACCP plan, particularly allergen changeover.
3. Trace incoming raw material batches to approved suppliers and required certificates of analysis.
4. Review third-party certification and regulator findings and verify corrective actions were implemented.
Red flags:
1. Monitoring records completed in identical handwriting at one time
2. Deviations released "on management authority"
3. Allergen changeover cleaning shortened to hit output
4. Supplier approvals lapsed but deliveries accepted
Evidence to request:
1. HACCP plans and CCP monitoring records
2. Deviation and disposition logs
3. Supplier approval files and certificates of analysis
4. Certification audit reports
Measures:
1. CCP deviations per period
2. % records complete
3. Overdue corrective actions

Sub-process: Asset Integrity and Safety Critical Maintenance
Risk: Safety-critical network maintenance is deferred, raising the risk of asset failure, supply interruption and public harm.
Why this matters: Utility assets carry public safety risk. Deferring maintenance to save money moves the cost to someone's injury.
Audit objective: Assess whether inspection and maintenance of safety-critical network assets is performed on schedule and defects are closed.
What to review:
1. Asset criticality classification and inspection intervals
2. Overdue safety-critical maintenance by asset class
3. Defect close-out and interim risk mitigation
4. Vegetation management and third-party interference
5. Contractor competency for high-risk work
Procedures:
1. Extract the maintenance plan and quantify overdue safety-critical tasks by asset class and region.
2. Trace a sample of high-priority defects to closure and verify the remediation physically occurred.
3. Test whether deferrals were formally risk-assessed and approved at the required level.
4. Review contractor competency and authorisation records for high-voltage or high-pressure work.
Red flags:
1. Deferrals approved in blocks at year end
2. Defects downgraded in priority without justification
3. Inspections recorded as complete with no field evidence
4. Contractors working outside their authorisation
Evidence to request:
1. Asset management system maintenance records
2. Defect registers
3. Deferral approvals
4. Contractor authorisation records
Measures:
1. Overdue safety-critical tasks
2. Defect close-out days
3. Unplanned outage frequency

Risk: Customers in financial hardship or on medical support are disconnected or pursued in breach of regulatory customer protection obligations.
Why this matters: Cutting off a customer who is ill or in hardship is a regulatory breach and a front-page story.
Audit objective: Confirm that customer protection obligations are applied before any restriction or disconnection.
What to review:
1. Identification and flagging of vulnerable and life-support customers
2. Hardship programme access and affordability assessment
3. Pre-disconnection notification and cooling-off requirements
4. Debt collection agency conduct
5. Complaint and ombudsman case outcomes
Procedures:
1. Reconcile disconnections executed against the vulnerable and life-support customer registers; investigate any overlap.
2. Test that each disconnection followed every required notification step within the prescribed timeframes.
3. Sample hardship applications and test the timeliness and consistency of assessment.
4. Review ombudsman and regulator determinations and trace systemic causes to remediation.
Red flags:
1. Life-support flags removed shortly before disconnection
2. Notification letters generated but not despatched
3. Hardship applications rejected at high rates by one team
4. Repeat ombudsman findings on the same issue
Evidence to request:
1. Disconnection records
2. Vulnerable customer registers
3. Hardship application files
4. Ombudsman and regulator correspondence
Measures:
1. Disconnections in breach
2. Hardship assessment turnaround
3. Ombudsman cases upheld

Sub-process: Revenue Leakage Across the Order to Cash Chain
Risk: Services are provisioned on the network but never reach billing, so the customer uses the service without ever being charged.
Why this matters: Every call or data session that never reaches billing is a service given away free.
Audit objective: Quantify revenue leakage between provisioning and billing and assess whether revenue assurance detects it.
What to review:
1. Reconciliation of network provisioning records to billing subscriptions
2. Free-of-charge and test accounts left active
3. Product catalogue consistency between systems
4. Discount and credit application
5. Revenue assurance coverage and independence
Procedures:
1. Reconcile active services on the network to active billing subscriptions; quantify the value of unbilled active services.
2. Extract free-of-charge, employee and test accounts and test whether each remains justified.
3. Compare product and tariff definitions across provisioning, rating and billing for inconsistencies.
4. Analyse credits and manual adjustments by user and reason code.
Red flags:
1. Test accounts with genuine consumption
2. Long-lived free-of-charge accounts
3. Catalogue changes made in one system only
4. Credits concentrated with a small number of users
Evidence to request:
1. Network provisioning extracts
2. Billing subscription data
3. Product catalogue configurations
4. Credit and adjustment logs
Measures:
1. Unbilled active services
2. Leakage as % of revenue
3. Credits per 1,000 subscribers

Risk: A poorly controlled network change causes a major service outage, with regulatory reporting obligations and customer compensation following.
Why this matters: A badly controlled network change can take service down for millions of customers, and that has to be reported to the regulator.
Audit objective: Assess whether network changes are controlled and whether resilience and recovery capability is proven rather than assumed.
What to review:
1. Change approval, testing and back-out planning
2. Emergency change usage and retrospective approval
3. Single points of failure in core network
4. Disaster recovery and failover testing
5. Major incident reporting to the regulator
Procedures:
1. Sample network changes and test for approval, testing evidence and a documented back-out plan.
2. Quantify emergency changes as a proportion of all changes and test whether retrospective approval occurred.
3. Review the most recent failover or disaster recovery test and confirm it exercised a genuine failover, not a tabletop walkthrough.
4. Trace major incidents to root-cause analysis, regulatory notification within the required window, and corrective action closure.
Red flags:
1. Emergency changes used routinely to bypass approval
2. Back-out plans stated as "restore from backup" with no detail
3. DR tests deferred or scoped to non-critical systems
4. Repeat incidents with the same root cause
Evidence to request:
1. Change management records
2. Emergency change log
3. DR test reports
4. Major incident and regulatory notification records
Measures:
1. Emergency changes as % of total
2. Change failure rate
3. Time to regulatory notification

Risk: Recorded inventory does not reflect what is physically held or what it is genuinely worth, misstating both the balance sheet and margin.
Why this matters: Stock is often the largest number on the balance sheet, and it is only worth what it can actually be sold for.
Audit objective: Verify that inventory exists, is owned, is counted accurately, and is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
What to review:
1. Count programme coverage, independence and adjustment approval
2. Goods in transit and consignment stock ownership
3. Cost build-up and overhead absorption
4. Net realisable value testing on slow-moving and damaged stock
5. Third-party locations and stock held by others
Procedures:
1. Attend counts at a sample of locations; re-perform test counts in both directions, floor to sheet and sheet to floor.
2. Test cut-off around the period end for goods received and despatched.
3. Obtain confirmations for stock held at third parties and reconcile to the ledger.
4. Recompute the cost build-up for a sample of items including overhead absorption, and compare cost to recent selling prices net of costs to sell.
5. Analyse adjustment postings for entries made outside the count process.
Red flags:
1. Adjustments posted just after a count to restore the book figure
2. Consignment stock recorded as owned
3. Overhead absorption rates unchanged despite volume shifts
4. Locations never selected for count
Evidence to request:
1. Inventory listings by location
2. Count sheets and adjustment postings
3. Third-party stock confirmations
4. Cost build-up files
5. Recent sales price data
Measures:
1. Count accuracy %
2. Adjustment value as % of inventory
3. Inventory turns

Risk: Capital spend is approved on optimistic business cases, overruns without escalation, and assets on the register can no longer be located.
Why this matters: Big capital projects get approved on promises, and almost nobody goes back to check whether the promises came true.
Audit objective: Assess whether capital investment is authorised, controlled against budget, and whether recorded assets physically exist.
What to review:
1. Business case quality and post-implementation review
2. Approval authority and project change control
3. Capitalisation timing and classification
4. Physical verification programme
5. Disposals, transfers and idle assets
Procedures:
1. Select major projects and compare approved business case benefits to post-implementation actuals; test whether reviews are performed at all.
2. Test overruns against the re-approval threshold and inspect evidence of escalation.
3. Physically verify a sample of recorded assets and, in reverse, trace observed assets back to the register.
4. Test the capitalisation date against evidence the asset was available for use.
5. Review idle and fully depreciated assets still in service for impairment or life reassessment.
Red flags:
1. Post-implementation reviews never performed
2. Projects split to stay under an approval threshold
3. Assets on the register nobody can locate
4. Capitalisation dated before commissioning
Evidence to request:
1. Capital approval papers and business cases
2. Project cost reports
3. Fixed asset register
4. Disposal records
Measures:
1. Capital spend vs. budget
2. % projects with post-implementation review
3. Assets verified / not located

Risk: Bank mandates, payment authority and hedging activity are not controlled, exposing the organisation to fraud and to unmanaged market risk.
Why this matters: Bank accounts and payment authority are the front door to the company's cash.
Audit objective: Confirm that banking arrangements, payment authority and treasury activity operate within board-approved mandates.
What to review:
1. Bank account inventory and signatory mandates
2. Payment release authority and dual authorisation
3. Treasury policy limits on counterparty, currency and interest exposure
4. Hedging authorisation and effectiveness
5. Cash forecasting accuracy and idle balances
Procedures:
1. Obtain a complete list of bank accounts from the banks themselves, not from the ledger, and reconcile to the recorded accounts.
2. Test current signatory mandates against the approved authority list and identify leavers still holding authority.
3. Test that payment release genuinely requires two independent approvers, including for urgent and manual payments.
4. Compare open treasury positions to policy limits at several dates and test breach escalation.
5. Compare cash forecasts to actuals and assess forecasting discipline.
Red flags:
1. Bank accounts not in the ledger
2. Leavers still on mandates
3. Urgent payments routinely bypassing dual authorisation
4. Positions repeatedly at or just inside limits
Evidence to request:
1. Bank confirmations and mandate letters
2. Payment system authority configuration
3. Treasury policy and position reports
4. Cash forecasts
Measures:
1. Accounts reconciled to bank confirmations
2. Payments released single-handed
3. Limit breaches per quarter

Risk: Returns are filed late or on incorrect positions, and intercompany pricing is not supported by documentation, leading to assessments, interest and penalties.
Why this matters: Filing tax late or on the wrong basis costs interest and penalties, and repeats every year until it is fixed.
Audit objective: Assess whether tax obligations are identified and met on time and whether positions taken are documented and defensible.
What to review:
1. Tax obligation calendar completeness across all jurisdictions
2. Filing and payment timeliness
3. Uncertain tax positions and provisioning
4. Transfer pricing policy, documentation and actual pricing applied
5. Indirect tax coding accuracy on transactions
Procedures:
1. Build the obligation calendar independently from entity and jurisdiction data and compare to the one in use.
2. Test filing and payment dates against statutory deadlines and quantify interest and penalties incurred.
3. Review uncertain tax positions and test whether the provision reflects current authority correspondence.
4. Test whether intercompany transactions were actually priced per the transfer pricing policy and whether local file documentation exists.
5. Sample transactions and re-perform indirect tax coding.
Red flags:
1. Obligations discovered only when the authority writes
2. Penalties recurring in the same jurisdiction
3. Transfer pricing documentation prepared long after year end
4. Manual overrides of tax codes at invoice entry
Evidence to request:
1. Tax obligation calendar
2. Filed returns and payment records
3. Authority correspondence and assessments
4. Transfer pricing documentation
Measures:
1. Filings on time %
2. Penalties and interest incurred
3. Jurisdictions with current TP documentation

Risk: Manual journal entries are used to force results to expectation, and the close is completed too quickly for controls to operate meaningfully.
Why this matters: Manual journals are how results get adjusted at the last minute, which makes them the first place to look.
Audit objective: Evaluate the integrity of the financial close, focusing on manual adjustments and account reconciliation quality.
What to review:
1. Manual journal authorisation, support and posting rights
2. Top-side and consolidation adjustments
3. Balance sheet reconciliation completion and review quality
4. Close timetable versus control operation
5. Estimates and accruals with judgement
Procedures:
1. Extract all manual journals and analyse by preparer, value, account, and posting date and time; test round-sum entries, entries posted at unusual hours, and entries to income statement accounts near period end.
2. Test that each sampled journal has support and an approver independent of the preparer.
3. Sample balance sheet reconciliations and reassess whether reconciling items are genuinely explained or simply labelled.
4. Compare journal patterns across periods to identify entries appearing only when results are close to target.
Red flags:
1. Journals posted after the close was reported as complete
2. Recurring entries with the description "reclass" and no support
3. Reconciliations signed the same day they were prepared
4. Late adjustments always moving in the favourable direction
Evidence to request:
1. Full journal entry extract with user and timestamp
2. Reconciliation files and sign-offs
3. Close timetable
4. Consolidation adjustment schedules
Measures:
1. Manual journals per period
2. % journals with support
3. Reconciliations overdue

Risk: Critical activities are outsourced without contractual protection, assurance over the provider, or a viable exit, so failures land back on the organisation.
Why this matters: Outsourcing the work never outsources the responsibility. When the supplier fails, it is still your problem.
Audit objective: Assess whether third parties performing critical activities are selected, contracted and monitored proportionately to the risk they carry.
What to review:
1. Inventory of third parties and criticality assessment
2. Due diligence performed before contracting
3. Contract terms — service levels, audit rights, data protection, exit
4. Ongoing assurance such as service auditor reports and site visits
5. Concentration risk and exit planning
Procedures:
1. Build an independent inventory of third parties from accounts payable and compare it to the register maintained by the business.
2. For critical providers, test that pre-contract due diligence was performed and documented.
3. Review contracts for audit rights, service levels, data protection and termination assistance.
4. Obtain service auditor reports for critical providers and test that complementary user controls were actually implemented.
5. Test whether exit plans exist and are credible for the most concentrated dependencies.
Red flags:
1. Critical providers absent from the register
2. Contracts auto-renewing without review
3. Service auditor reports received but never read
4. Exceptions in those reports with no follow-up
5. No alternative provider identified for a single point of dependency
Evidence to request:
1. Accounts payable vendor spend
2. Third-party register and criticality ratings
3. Contracts
4. Service auditor reports
5. Exit plans
Measures:
1. % critical providers with current due diligence
2. Contracts with audit rights
3. Assurance reports reviewed

Risk: People are hired without verification of their credentials, retain access and entitlements after leaving, and exit obligations are not enforced.
Why this matters: Hiring someone without checking who they are, and letting leavers keep access, are both simple failures with expensive consequences.
Audit objective: Assess whether the employee lifecycle is controlled from pre-hire screening through to exit.
What to review:
1. Pre-employment screening — identity, right to work, qualifications, references, criminal record where permitted
2. Approval of new positions against approved headcount
3. Onboarding: contract, code of conduct, mandatory training
4. Exit: access removal, asset return, final pay, restrictive covenants
5. Contractor and contingent worker treatment
Procedures:
1. Sample new hires and test that every required screening step was completed before the start date, not after.
2. Verify professional qualifications directly with the issuing body for roles where they are a condition of employment.
3. Reconcile headcount to approved positions and investigate roles filled without approval.
4. Sample leavers and test the elapsed time to access removal, asset return and final settlement.
5. Test whether contractors are subject to equivalent screening for equivalent access.
Red flags:
1. Screening completed weeks after the start date
2. Qualifications accepted on a photocopy
3. Leavers retaining building or system access
4. Contractors engaged for years through rolling short contracts
5. Exit interviews not conducted for regretted leavers
Evidence to request:
1. Employee files and screening records
2. Headcount approvals
3. Joiner and leaver reports
4. Asset registers
5. Contractor engagement records
Measures:
1. % hires fully screened before start
2. Days to remove leaver access
3. Contractor tenure distribution

Risk: Pay decisions, incentives and promotions are made inconsistently, and behavioural issues are not addressed, driving turnover, grievance and conduct risk.
Why this matters: How people are paid and promoted drives how they behave, which shapes every other control in the business.
Audit objective: Evaluate whether reward and performance processes are applied consistently and whether conduct concerns are dealt with.
What to review:
1. Salary review and promotion decision governance
2. Incentive plan design and payout calculation
3. Pay equity across comparable roles
4. Performance management completion and quality
5. Grievance, disciplinary and harassment case handling
Procedures:
1. Recompute a sample of incentive payouts against plan rules and approved performance outcomes.
2. Analyse pay across comparable roles for unexplained dispersion, and test the explanations offered.
3. Test performance review completion rates and read a sample for substance rather than box-ticking.
4. Review grievance and disciplinary cases for investigation independence, timeliness and consistency of outcome.
5. Compare voluntary turnover by manager and function against the organisational average.
Red flags:
1. Incentives paid despite unmet performance conditions
2. Turnover concentrated under specific managers
3. Grievances against senior staff investigated by their own reports
4. Performance ratings clustered with no differentiation
Evidence to request:
1. Payroll and incentive calculation files
2. Performance review records
3. Grievance and disciplinary case files
4. Turnover and exit interview data
Measures:
1. Voluntary turnover by manager
2. % reviews completed
3. Grievance cases and outcomes

Risk: Cargo loss and damage claims are settled without investigating root cause or pursuing recovery from the carrier at fault, so the same losses recur.
Why this matters: Cargo claims get paid without checking whether another party was actually at fault and should be paying instead.
Audit objective: Assess whether claims are validated, recovered where a third party is liable, and used to drive corrective action.
What to review:
1. Claim intake, validation and settlement authority
2. Evidence required before settlement — proof of delivery, condition reports, photographs
3. Recovery from subcontracted carriers and insurers
4. Root-cause analysis and corrective action on repeat loss points
5. Claims reserve adequacy and ageing
Procedures:
1. Sample settled claims and test that liability was established before payment, not assumed.
2. Identify claims where a subcontracted carrier held the freight at the time of loss and test whether recovery was pursued within the contractual notice period.
3. Analyse claims by terminal, lane and commodity to locate concentrations, then test whether any corrective action followed.
4. Test the ageing of open claims and the basis for the reserve held against them.
5. Reconcile the claims register to the general ledger loss account and to insurer recoveries.
Red flags:
1. Claims settled below an investigation threshold that is never reviewed in aggregate
2. Recovery notice periods missed repeatedly
3. The same terminal appearing in loss concentrations quarter after quarter
4. Claims paid without proof of delivery on file
Evidence to request:
1. Claims register with reserve history
2. OS&D incident logs
3. Subcontract carrier agreements and notice terms
4. Insurer correspondence and recovery records
Measures:
1. Claims paid vs. recovered
2. Loss per million shipments
3. Repeat loss locations

Risk: Gift card and loyalty balances are manipulated by staff, or breakage is recognised on an assumption that overstates income.
Why this matters: Gift cards and loyalty points are money the business owes customers. Assuming too much of it will never be claimed flatters profit.
Audit objective: Assess the integrity of stored-value and loyalty balances and the support for breakage recognition.
What to review:
1. Gift card activation, reload and void controls at the till
2. Loyalty point issuance, adjustment and manual accrual rights
3. Breakage assumption and redemption history supporting it
4. Reconciliation of the liability to the issuing platform
5. Employee accounts and their transaction patterns
Procedures:
1. Analyse gift card activations reversed or voided shortly after issue, by operator.
2. Test manual loyalty point adjustments by user and value; sample the largest for approval and business reason.
3. Match loyalty and gift card accounts to employee records and analyse redemption behaviour on those accounts.
4. Recompute breakage using the actual redemption curve and compare to the rate recognised.
5. Reconcile the platform balance to the ledger liability at several dates.
Red flags:
1. Cards activated and voided in the same shift
2. Points adjusted upward immediately before redemption
3. Employee-linked accounts with outsized balances
4. Breakage rate unchanged for years despite behaviour shifts
Evidence to request:
1. Gift card and loyalty platform transaction data
2. Point adjustment logs
3. Employee master data
4. Liability reconciliations
Measures:
1. Void rate by operator
2. Manual point adjustments
3. Breakage as % of issuance

Risk: Payments are processed to incorrect or fraudulent beneficiaries, and internal or dormant accounts are used to warehouse the proceeds.
Why this matters: Payments are where money physically leaves the bank, so this is the step a fraudster most wants to control.
Audit objective: Assess controls over payment execution, beneficiary integrity and the use of internal and dormant accounts.
What to review:
1. Payment authorisation limits and dual control by channel
2. Beneficiary verification and confirmation-of-payee checks
3. Dormant account reactivation and monitoring
4. Internal, suspense and staff account usage
5. Payment recall and error correction process
Procedures:
1. Test that every payment channel enforces dual authorisation at the stated thresholds, including manual and urgent routes.
2. Analyse dormant accounts that reactivated in the period and test the first transaction on each.
3. Extract transactions on internal and staff accounts and test the business justification for the largest and most frequent.
4. Sample high-value payments and test beneficiary verification evidence.
5. Review payment errors and recalls for pattern and for whether root causes were fixed.
Red flags:
1. Urgent payments bypassing dual control
2. Dormant accounts reactivating just before a large credit
3. Staff accounts transacting with customer accounts
4. Beneficiary details changed shortly before payment release
Evidence to request:
1. Payment system transaction logs and authorisation configuration
2. Dormant account reports
3. Internal and staff account statements
4. Payment error and recall register
Measures:
1. Payments released single-handed
2. Dormant reactivations investigated
3. Error and recall rate

Risk: Aircraft are returned to lessors without meeting contractual return conditions, triggering large end-of-lease compensation claims that were never provided for.
Why this matters: Leased aircraft must be given back in a specified condition. That bill arrives years after the decisions that caused it.
Audit objective: Assess whether lease return obligations are tracked through the lease term and provided for on a supportable basis.
What to review:
1. Inventory of lease return conditions per aircraft
2. Tracking of maintenance status against those conditions
3. Provisioning for expected return costs
4. Records and back-to-birth traceability required at return
5. Negotiation and settlement of end-of-lease claims
Procedures:
1. Build a register of return conditions from the lease agreements themselves and compare it to what the business is tracking.
2. For aircraft returning within two years, compare current maintenance status to the required return condition and quantify the gap.
3. Test whether the provision reflects that gap or only scheduled maintenance.
4. Review recent lease returns and compare final settlement to the amount provided.
5. Test the completeness of component records required at return.
Red flags:
1. Return conditions summarised by the operator rather than read from the lease
2. Provisions based on maintenance plans, not lease terms
3. Settlements consistently exceeding provisions
4. Component records reconstructed close to the return date
Evidence to request:
1. Lease agreements and return condition schedules
2. Maintenance status reports by aircraft
3. Provision calculations
4. Prior lease return settlements
Measures:
1. Aircraft with quantified return gaps
2. Settlement vs. provision variance
3. Records completeness at return

Risk: Fare rules, refunds and interline settlements are applied incorrectly, so revenue is lost between the booking and the general ledger.
Why this matters: A ticket sold is not money earned until the passenger flies. Mixing those two up overstates revenue.
Audit objective: Assess whether flown revenue is complete and correctly valued, and whether refunds and interline balances are controlled.
What to review:
1. Fare rule configuration and manual fare overrides
2. Refund and reissue authority and reason codes
3. Interline and code-share settlement reconciliation
4. Agency and distribution channel commission accuracy
5. Unflown ticket expiry and residual value treatment
Procedures:
1. Re-price a sample of tickets from the fare rules and quantify variance to the fare actually charged.
2. Analyse refunds and reissues by agent and reason code; sample the outliers for authorisation.
3. Reconcile interline billings to the settlement clearing house statements and test disputes raised within the deadline.
4. Recompute agency commission for a sample against the distribution agreement.
5. Test the expiry and recognition of unflown tickets against the stated policy.
Red flags:
1. Manual fare overrides concentrated with a few agents
2. Refunds issued to a payment method other than the original
3. Interline disputes filed after the deadline
4. Expiry recognition accelerated near period end
Evidence to request:
1. Revenue accounting system extracts
2. Fare rule configuration
3. Refund and reissue logs
4. Clearing house settlement statements
Measures:
1. Fare variance on re-pricing
2. Refunds by agent
3. Interline disputes recovered

Risk: Food and beverage margin is lost through unrecorded wastage, over-portioning, unauthorised staff meals and supplier short-delivery.
Why this matters: More drink leaves the bottle than the till records, and the gap is usually explained away as waste.
Audit objective: Identify where margin is lost between purchase and sale in food and beverage outlets.
What to review:
1. Recipe costing and portion control
2. Wastage recording and its plausibility
3. Staff meal and entertainment policy and recording
4. Goods receipt verification against delivery notes and weights
5. Void and discount patterns in the outlet point of sale
Procedures:
1. Observe service and compare actual portions to the costed recipe for high-volume items.
2. Compare recorded wastage across outlets and shifts; implausibly low or perfectly consistent wastage warrants challenge.
3. Test goods receipt for weight and count verification rather than signature only, for a sample of deliveries.
4. Analyse voids, discounts and staff meals by server and shift against outlet averages.
5. Reconcile theoretical to actual consumption for a sample of high-value beverage lines.
Red flags:
1. Wastage recorded as the same figure every week
2. Deliveries signed without verification
3. Discounts concentrated on particular shifts
4. Stock counts performed by the outlet manager alone
Evidence to request:
1. Recipe and costing files
2. Wastage logs
3. Goods receipt records and delivery notes
4. Point of sale transaction data
Measures:
1. Pour cost variance
2. Wastage as % of purchases
3. Discounts per server

Risk: Fuel uplifted into aircraft is not reconciled to supplier invoices, so the airline pays for volumes it never received.
Why this matters: Fuel is one of the largest costs an airline has, and nobody stands at the wing checking the litres against the invoice unless someone makes them.
Audit objective: Confirm that fuel purchased reconciles to fuel uplifted and that pricing follows the supply contract.
What to review:
1. Uplift recording at the wing and its independence from the supplier
2. Reconciliation of uplift tickets to supplier invoices
3. Contract pricing, differentials and into-plane fees
4. Density and temperature correction on volumes
5. Dispute handling with fuel suppliers
Procedures:
1. Reconcile uplift volumes from flight records to supplier invoiced volumes by station and quantify the difference.
2. Re-price a sample of invoices against the contract, including index differentials and into-plane fees.
3. Test whether volume corrections for temperature and density were applied consistently.
4. Review the ageing and outcome of fuel supplier disputes.
Red flags:
1. Uplift recorded solely from the supplier ticket
2. Persistent one-directional variances at a station
3. Fees charged that are not in the contract
4. Disputes abandoned rather than resolved
Evidence to request:
1. Flight records and uplift tickets
2. Fuel supplier invoices
3. Fuel supply contracts
4. Dispute correspondence
Measures:
1. Uplift-to-invoice variance
2. Price variance to contract
3. Disputes recovered

Risk: Orders are picked, packed or shipped incorrectly, generating replacement cost, refunds and customer loss that is absorbed as a cost of doing business.
Why this matters: Every order picked wrong costs the replacement, the delivery and often the customer.
Audit objective: Assess fulfilment accuracy, the cost of getting it wrong, and whether root causes are addressed.
What to review:
1. Pick and pack accuracy and verification at despatch
2. Inventory accuracy between the warehouse and the storefront
3. Carrier performance and lost parcel handling
4. Replacement and refund cost attribution
5. Returns processing and restocking accuracy
Procedures:
1. Quantify order defects — wrong item, missing item, damaged — and the total cost of remediation over the period.
2. Test inventory accuracy by cycle count and compare to the availability shown on the storefront; oversell indicates a control gap.
3. Analyse lost and damaged parcels by carrier and test whether claims were filed within the carrier deadline.
4. Trace a sample of returns from receipt to restock or write-off and test the valuation applied.
Red flags:
1. Defect cost recorded in a general expense account with no attribution
2. Overselling followed by silent cancellation
3. Carrier claims not filed
4. Returned stock restocked without inspection
Evidence to request:
1. Order defect and remediation records
2. Cycle count results
3. Carrier performance and claims data
4. Returns processing records
Measures:
1. Order defect rate
2. Remediation cost per order
3. Carrier claim recovery %

Risk: Third-party sellers list counterfeit, unsafe or prohibited products, exposing the platform to regulatory action and liability.
Why this matters: On a marketplace, the platform is judged by what its sellers list, including counterfeit or unsafe goods.
