2. Insurance lapse exceptions
3. % spend with conditional-rated carriers

Risk: Payments are made to fictitious vendors, or to genuine vendors at bank details altered by a fraudster.
Why this matters: Payments to suppliers are the most common route for money to leave a company fraudulently.
Audit objective: Determine whether vendor master changes are independently verified and whether the payment population contains indicators of fraud or duplication.
What to review:
1. Vendor creation and bank change verification
2. Segregation between vendor maintenance, invoice entry and payment release
3. Duplicate payment detection
4. Employee-to-vendor data matching
5. Dormant vendor reactivation
Procedures:
1. Match the vendor master against the employee master on bank account, address, tax ID and phone number.
2. Test all bank detail changes in the period for evidence of independent call-back verification to a number obtained from an independent source.
3. Run duplicate payment analytics on invoice number, amount, date and vendor across near-matches.
4. Identify vendors reactivated after long dormancy and test the first payment after reactivation.
5. Test system access to confirm no user can both maintain the vendor and release the payment.
Red flags:
1. Bank change immediately followed by a large payment
2. Vendors sharing a bank account
3. Invoices just below the approval threshold
4. Vendor address matching an employee address
Evidence to request:
1. Vendor master change log
2. Employee master
3. Payment run files
4. ERP access and role assignments
Measures:
1. Duplicate payments recovered
2. % bank changes with verified call-back
3. Vendor master exception count

Risk: Users retain access after role change or termination, or hold combinations of access that allow a transaction to be initiated and approved by the same person.
Why this matters: People who change jobs or leave often keep their old system access, which is how small problems become large ones.
Audit objective: Assess whether logical access is granted, reviewed and removed in line with role requirements and segregation of duties rules.
What to review:
1. Joiner, mover and leaver processing
2. Periodic user access recertification
3. Privileged and generic account use
4. Segregation of duties conflict matrix
5. Access to production data and direct database changes
Procedures:
1. Reconcile active system accounts to the active employee list; test every orphan account.
2. Measure elapsed days from termination to access removal across all leavers in the period.
3. Run the SoD conflict matrix against current role assignments and quantify unmitigated conflicts.
4. Test whether the last recertification was completed by the business owner and whether flagged removals actually occurred.
5. Review privileged account activity logs for direct data changes outside change management.
Red flags:
1. Recertification approved in bulk on a single day
2. Generic accounts shared by a team
3. Firefighter access left permanently enabled
4. Removals flagged but never executed
Evidence to request:
1. User access listings by system
2. HR joiner/leaver data
3. Recertification evidence
4. Privileged activity logs
Measures:
1. Days to revoke access
2. Unmitigated SoD conflicts
3. % accounts recertified on time

Risk: Concerns raised through the ethics line are not investigated independently, or undisclosed conflicts of interest influence supplier selection.
Why this matters: If people do not trust the confidential reporting line, management is the last to know about problems.
Audit objective: Evaluate whether the ethics reporting channel is trusted and effective, and whether conflicts of interest are disclosed and managed.
What to review:
1. Ethics line availability, anonymity and awareness
2. Case triage, investigation independence and closure
3. Conflict of interest declaration completeness
4. Related-party transactions with declared interests
5. Retaliation monitoring
Procedures:
1. Review the case log for volume, category, ageing and closure quality; test a sample end to end.
2. Test whether cases implicating management were investigated by someone outside that reporting line.
3. Reconcile conflict of interest declarations to the employee population and test completeness for decision-makers.
4. Match declared interests against the vendor master and investigate transactions with connected parties.
Red flags:
1. Very low case volume relative to headcount
2. Cases closed as unsubstantiated with no documented work
3. Declarations missing from procurement and finance staff
4. Reporters subsequently exiting the business
Evidence to request:
1. Ethics case management log
2. Conflict of interest declarations
3. Vendor master
4. Exit interview records
Measures:
1. Cases per 1,000 employees
2. Average days to close
3. % declarations completed

Sub-process: Third Party Inventory and Risk Tiering
Risk: The organisation does not know who its third parties are or which matter, so oversight is applied to the wrong ones.
Why this matters: You cannot manage suppliers you do not know you have, and most companies have more than they think.
Audit objective: Confirm third parties are identified completely and tiered by the risk they present.
What to review:
1. Completeness of the third-party register against payments and system access
2. Criticality and risk tiering methodology
3. Fourth-party and subcontracting visibility
4. Ownership of each relationship inside the business
5. Refresh of tiering when the service changes
Procedures:
1. Build an independent third-party inventory from accounts payable and system access data and compare it to the register.
2. Test the tiering of a sample against the methodology; challenge any critical service tiered low.
3. Test whether subcontracting by key providers is known and permitted by contract.
4. Test that each relationship has a named business owner.
Red flags:
1. Providers paid regularly but absent from the register
2. Critical services tiered as low risk
3. No knowledge of who the provider subcontracts to
4. Relationships with no owner since the manager left
Evidence to request:
1. Accounts payable vendor data
2. Third-party register and tiering
3. System access listings
4. Contracts
Measures:
1. Providers not in register
2. Critical providers tiered
3. Relationships with named owner

Risk: Third parties are engaged without checks on their financial health, integrity or capability, and problems surface only after dependency exists.
Why this matters: Checking a supplier after you depend on them is too late to do anything about what you find.
Audit objective: Confirm due diligence is performed before engagement and is proportionate to risk.
What to review:
1. Due diligence scope by risk tier — financial, sanctions, integrity, capability
2. Timing — before contract signature or after
3. Sanctions, anti-bribery and modern slavery screening
4. Site visits or technical assessment for critical providers
5. Refresh of due diligence during the relationship
Procedures:
1. Test that due diligence was completed before contract signature for a sample of engagements.
2. Test screening evidence for sanctions and adverse media on critical providers.
3. Test the currency of due diligence for long-standing relationships.
4. Assess whether financial health of critical providers is monitored, not just checked once.
Red flags:
1. Due diligence dated after the contract
2. Long relationships never re-assessed
3. Screening limited to a search engine query
4. Financial distress at a provider discovered from the news
Evidence to request:
1. Due diligence files
2. Screening records
3. Contracts and signature dates
4. Financial monitoring records
Measures:
1. DD before signature %
2. Critical providers refreshed
3. Screening completed

Risk: Contracts omit the protections the organisation needs, so there is no remedy when the provider fails.
Why this matters: The contract is the only leverage you have when a supplier fails. Missing terms means no remedy.
Audit objective: Confirm contracts contain the terms required for the risk the provider carries.
What to review:
1. Presence of service levels, remedies and service credits
2. Audit and inspection rights
3. Data protection, confidentiality and security obligations
4. Liability caps, indemnities and insurance requirements
5. Termination, exit assistance and transition obligations
Procedures:
1. Review contracts for critical providers against a required-terms checklist and quantify gaps.
2. Test whether spend is occurring under expired or absent contracts.
3. Test whether liability caps are proportionate to the exposure the service creates.
4. Test whether audit rights have ever been exercised.
Red flags:
1. Material spend with no signed contract
2. Liability capped at one month of fees for a critical service
3. Auto-renewal with no review point
4. Audit rights present but never used
Evidence to request:
1. Contract register and agreements
2. Spend analysis
3. Insurance certificates
4. Renewal records
Measures:
1. Spend under contract %
2. Contracts with audit rights
3. Expired contracts still active

Risk: Provider performance is not measured, so service degrades and contractual remedies go unclaimed.
Why this matters: If nobody measures the service, it drifts, and the credits you were owed are never claimed.
Audit objective: Confirm provider performance is measured against contract and managed actively.
What to review:
1. Service level definition and who measures performance
2. Provider self-reporting versus independent measurement
3. Service credit and remedy claims
4. Governance meetings, minutes and escalation
5. Relationship between performance and contract renewal
Procedures:
1. Test whether performance data is produced by the provider or independently verified.
2. Recompute service levels for a sample of periods and test whether credits due were claimed.
3. Review governance meeting minutes for substance and escalation of persistent failures.
4. Test whether poor performers were renewed regardless.
Red flags:
1. Performance reported solely by the provider
2. Service credits never claimed
3. Governance meetings cancelled repeatedly
4. Consistently failing providers renewed
Evidence to request:
1. Service level reports
2. Contracts and credit provisions
3. Governance minutes
4. Renewal decisions
Measures:
1. SLA attainment
2. Credits claimed vs. due
3. Governance meetings held

Risk: The organisation relies on controls operated by a third party without any evidence that they work.
Why this matters: When a supplier performs a control for you, you still have to prove it works.
Audit objective: Confirm assurance is obtained over provider controls and acted upon.
What to review:
1. Assurance strategy by tier — service auditor reports, certifications, right to audit
2. Review of reports received, including exceptions and qualified opinions
3. Complementary user entity controls and whether they are performed
4. Coverage gaps between report period and financial year
5. Escalation of adverse findings
Procedures:
1. Obtain service auditor reports for critical providers; test whether anyone read them by tracing exceptions to management action.
2. Identify complementary user entity controls and test whether the organisation performs each.
3. Test the coverage period against the financial year and how gaps are addressed.
4. Assess reliance placed on certifications that do not cover the services actually used.
Red flags:
1. Reports filed unread
2. Complementary controls never identified
3. Certification scope excluding the service used
4. Qualified opinions with no response
Evidence to request:
1. Service auditor reports and certifications
2. Bridge letters
3. Complementary control testing
4. Management responses
Measures:
1. Critical providers with assurance
2. Complementary controls tested
3. Exceptions addressed

Risk: Third parties hold or access the organisation's data without adequate protection, and a breach at the provider becomes the organisation's breach.
Why this matters: A data breach at your supplier is reported as your data breach.
Audit objective: Confirm data shared with third parties is protected, minimised and governed.
What to review:
1. Inventory of data shared with each provider and its classification
2. Processor agreements and lawful basis for transfers
3. Security requirements imposed and verified
4. Provider access into the organisation's environment
5. Breach notification obligations and testing of the route
Procedures:
1. Reconcile providers receiving personal or sensitive data to signed processor agreements.
2. Test the security requirements imposed on providers and any verification performed.
3. Test provider access accounts — authentication, privilege, monitoring and removal.
4. Test whether breach notification routes have been exercised or are theoretical.
Red flags:
1. Data shared with no agreement in place
2. Provider staff with standing privileged access
3. Security requirements stated but never verified
4. No test of the breach notification path
Evidence to request:
1. Data sharing inventory
2. Processor agreements
3. Provider access listings
4. Security assessment records
Measures:
1. Providers with agreements
2. Provider access reviewed
3. Security verifications performed

Risk: A critical provider fails and there is no alternative and no exit plan, so the disruption is unbounded.
Why this matters: If a critical supplier fails and there is no alternative, the disruption lasts as long as it lasts.
Audit objective: Assess whether dependency on third parties is understood and survivable.
What to review:
1. Concentration analysis — single providers, shared fourth parties, geographic concentration
2. Business continuity requirements imposed and tested with the provider
3. Exit plans, transition assistance and data return
4. Substitutability of each critical provider
5. Testing of failover to an alternative
Procedures:
1. Identify critical services with a single provider and no substitute, and test the mitigation.
2. Test whether continuity arrangements have been jointly exercised with the provider.
3. Review exit plans for credibility — timescale, cost, data format, resource.
4. Analyse fourth-party concentration where several providers depend on the same underlying supplier.
Red flags:
1. Exit plan consisting of a single paragraph
2. Continuity never tested with the provider
3. Several critical providers hosted on the same platform
4. Data held in a proprietary format with no export
Evidence to request:
1. Concentration analysis
2. Continuity test records
3. Exit plans
4. Provider architecture information
Measures:
1. Critical services single-sourced
2. Continuity tests performed
3. Exit plans credible

Risk: Work performed offshore creates regulatory, tax and resilience exposure that was never assessed.
Why this matters: Moving work to another country brings regulatory, tax and oversight issues that are easy to miss.
Audit objective: Confirm cross-border service arrangements comply with regulatory and data residency requirements.
What to review:
1. Regulatory notification or approval requirements for outsourcing
2. Data residency and cross-border transfer mechanisms
3. Local labour, tax and permanent establishment considerations
4. Time zone, language and oversight practicality
5. Geopolitical and country risk assessment
Procedures:
1. Test whether required regulatory notifications for outsourcing were made.
2. Test data residency against the contractual and regulatory requirement.
3. Assess whether offshore arrangements create permanent establishment or transfer pricing exposure.
4. Test the practical oversight exercised over offshore operations.
Red flags:
1. Outsourcing arrangements never notified to the regulator
2. Data processed in jurisdictions not permitted
3. No country risk assessment for concentrated locations
4. Oversight limited to a monthly call
Evidence to request:
1. Outsourcing agreements
2. Regulatory notifications
3. Data flow mapping
4. Country risk assessments
Measures:
1. Notifications made
2. Data residency exceptions
3. Offshore sites visited

Risk: The board and its committees lack the information, independence or challenge to oversee the organisation effectively.
Why this matters: The board is the last line of defence. If it cannot see problems or will not challenge, nothing else compensates.
Audit objective: Assess whether governance arrangements provide genuine oversight.
What to review:
1. Board and committee composition, independence and skills
2. Quality, timeliness and balance of information provided
3. Evidence of challenge in minutes
4. Committee terms of reference and coverage of their remit
5. Board evaluation and succession planning
Procedures:
1. Review minutes across several meetings for evidence of challenge, dissent and follow-up, not just approval.
2. Test whether papers reached members with enough time to read them.
3. Test committee coverage against terms of reference — matters required but never discussed.
4. Assess whether management reporting to the board matches what the audit found operationally.
Red flags:
1. Minutes recording approval with no discussion
2. Papers issued the day before
3. Terms of reference matters never on any agenda
4. Board evaluation never performed
Evidence to request:
1. Board and committee minutes and packs
2. Terms of reference
3. Composition and independence records
4. Evaluation reports
Measures:
1. Papers issued on time
2. Matters covered vs. remit
3. Actions closed

Sub-process: Tone at the Top and Culture
Risk: Stated values are contradicted by what management rewards and tolerates, so controls are undermined from above.
Why this matters: People take their cue from what leaders reward and tolerate, not from what the policy says.
Audit objective: Assess whether the culture supports the control environment in practice, not only in policy.
What to review:
1. Code of conduct, its communication and acknowledgement
2. Consistency between stated values and incentive design
3. Consequence management — how breaches by senior staff are handled
4. Speak-up culture and psychological safety indicators
5. Employee survey results relevant to ethics and pressure
Procedures:
1. Compare disciplinary outcomes for similar breaches at different seniority levels.
2. Test whether incentive plans reward outcomes the code discourages.
3. Review survey data for indicators of pressure to meet targets at any cost, and follow up on the worst-scoring units.
4. Interview staff at multiple levels about whether they would raise a concern and what they expect would happen.
Red flags:
1. Senior breaches handled quietly while junior ones are dismissed
2. Targets that can only be met by cutting corners
3. Survey scores on ethics declining with no response
4. Exit interviews citing pressure repeatedly
Evidence to request:
1. Code of conduct and acknowledgements
2. Disciplinary case records
3. Incentive plan documents
4. Employee survey and exit interview data
Measures:
1. Code acknowledgement rate
2. Consistency of consequence
3. Survey ethics scores

Risk: Risk management is a reporting exercise disconnected from decisions, so real risks are absent from the register.
Why this matters: If the risk register does not contain the things that actually go wrong, risk management is decoration.
Audit objective: Assess whether the risk framework identifies and manages the risks that actually threaten the organisation.
What to review:
1. Risk appetite definition and its use in decisions
2. Risk identification process and register completeness
3. Assessment methodology and consistency of scoring
4. Mitigation ownership, action tracking and effectiveness
5. Emerging risk identification and horizon scanning
Procedures:
1. Compare the risk register to issues identified by audit, incidents and losses — gaps show the identification process is not working.
2. Test whether risk appetite has ever caused a decision to change.
3. Test the scoring of a sample for consistency and challenge.
4. Test whether mitigation actions were completed and made a difference.
Red flags:
1. Risks scored to sit just inside appetite
2. Register unchanged for years
3. Incidents occurring in areas rated low risk
4. Mitigation actions perpetually in progress
Evidence to request:
1. Risk register and appetite statement
2. Incident and loss data
3. Risk committee minutes
4. Action tracking
Measures:
1. Register vs. incidents alignment
2. Actions overdue
3. Risks outside appetite

Risk: Policies are out of date, contradictory or unknown to the people expected to follow them.
Why this matters: A policy nobody knows about or follows provides no protection, only the appearance of it.
Audit objective: Confirm the policy framework is current, accessible and complied with.
What to review:
1. Policy inventory, ownership and review cycle
2. Accessibility and communication to affected staff
3. Consistency between related policies
4. Attestation and training completion
5. Monitoring of actual compliance rather than assumed compliance
Procedures:
1. Test the policy inventory for overdue reviews and identify policies referencing superseded regulation.
2. Test staff awareness of key policies in the areas audited.
3. Test attestation and training completion, particularly for high-risk roles.
4. Compare policy requirements to observed practice in the processes audited.
Red flags:
1. Policies years past review date
2. Practice diverging from policy with no exception recorded
3. Training completion tracked but not enforced
4. Contradictory requirements in related policies
Evidence to request:
1. Policy inventory and documents
2. Training and attestation records
3. Process observations
4. Exception approvals
Measures:
1. Policies within review cycle
2. Training completion
3. Policy vs. practice gaps

Risk: Authority limits are unclear, outdated or unenforced, so decisions are made by people without the mandate.
Why this matters: If it is unclear who can approve what, decisions get made by people without the authority to make them.
Audit objective: Confirm delegated authority is defined, current and enforced in the systems where it matters.
What to review:
1. Currency of the delegation of authority matrix
2. Alignment between the matrix and system configuration
3. Delegation during absence and its expiry
4. Authority held by leavers and movers
5. Evidence of decisions taken outside authority
Procedures:
1. Compare the delegation matrix to system approval limits in the finance, procurement and HR systems and quantify differences.
2. Test delegations granted during absence for expiry.
3. Reconcile approvers active in systems to current role holders.
4. Test a sample of significant decisions against the authority held at the time.
Red flags:
1. System limits inconsistent with the matrix
2. Temporary delegations never revoked
3. Leavers still active as approvers
4. Matrix last updated after a reorganisation two years ago
Evidence to request:
1. Delegation of authority matrix
2. System approval configuration
3. HR role data
4. Approval records
Measures:
1. Matrix to system alignment
2. Expired delegations active
3. Decisions outside authority

Risk: Fraud risk is assumed to be covered by other controls, so no one assesses where the organisation is actually exposed.
Why this matters: Fraud does not get prevented by general controls. Someone has to think specifically about how it would be done here.
Audit objective: Assess whether fraud risk is specifically assessed, mitigated and detected.
What to review:
1. Fraud risk assessment covering asset misappropriation, corruption and financial reporting fraud
2. Ownership of fraud risk and specific anti-fraud controls
3. Fraud detection analytics and their coverage
4. Investigation capability, independence and consistency
5. Loss recording, recovery and lessons applied
Procedures:
1. Test whether a fraud risk assessment exists and covers the schemes relevant to the business, not generic categories.
2. Test the anti-fraud controls claimed against each significant scheme.
3. Review investigations for independence, quality and consistency of outcome.
4. Test whether identified frauds led to control changes.
Red flags:
1. Fraud risk assessment copied from a template
2. Investigations conducted by the function investigated
3. Losses written off without root cause work
4. No detective analytics in high-risk processes
Evidence to request:
1. Fraud risk assessment
2. Investigation files
3. Loss register
4. Analytics coverage documentation
Measures:
1. Schemes assessed
2. Investigations independent
3. Controls changed after fraud

Risk: Concerns are not raised or not acted upon, and undisclosed interests influence decisions.
Why this matters: If raising a concern feels unsafe, management finds out about problems from the regulator or the press instead.
Audit objective: Assess whether the speak-up channel is trusted and effective and whether conflicts are managed.
What to review:
1. Channel availability, anonymity, independence and awareness
2. Case triage, investigation independence and closure quality
3. Conflict of interest declarations — completeness and refresh
4. Management of declared conflicts, not just declaration
5. Retaliation monitoring
Procedures:
1. Analyse case volume against benchmarks for organisation size; very low volume indicates a channel people do not trust.
2. Test cases implicating senior management for investigator independence.
3. Reconcile conflict declarations to the population required to declare, particularly procurement, finance and hiring managers.
4. Test what happened after a conflict was declared — management action, not just a record.
Red flags:
1. Case volume near zero
2. Cases closed as unsubstantiated with no documented work
3. Declarations collected but never acted on
4. Reporters leaving shortly after raising a concern
Evidence to request:
1. Case management records
2. Conflict declarations and registers
3. Investigation files
4. Exit interview data
Measures:
1. Cases per 1,000 staff
2. Days to close
3. Declarations completed

Risk: Regulatory obligations are not identified or tracked to an owner, so breaches are found by the regulator.
Why this matters: Regulatory obligations that nobody owns get missed, and being told by the regulator is the expensive way to find out.
Audit objective: Confirm regulatory obligations are identified, owned, monitored and evidenced.
What to review:
1. Completeness of the regulatory obligation inventory
2. Horizon scanning for new and changing requirements
3. Ownership and monitoring of each obligation
4. Breach identification, self-reporting and remediation
5. Regulatory relationship and correspondence handling
Procedures:
1. Build an obligation list independently for the most significant regulations and compare to the inventory.
2. Test evidence of compliance for a sample of obligations rather than an assertion.
3. Test breach self-reporting timeliness and remediation delivery.
4. Test whether regulatory change was assessed and implemented on time.
Red flags:
1. Obligations with no owner
2. Compliance asserted with no evidence
3. Regulatory change implemented after the deadline
4. Breaches identified externally first
Evidence to request:
1. Obligation inventory
2. Regulatory correspondence
3. Breach register
4. Change implementation records
Measures:
1. Obligations with evidence
2. Breaches self-identified
3. Change implemented on time

Risk: The organisation cannot continue operating through disruption because plans are theoretical and untested.
Why this matters: Plans that have never been tested tend not to work when they are finally needed.
Audit objective: Assess whether continuity and crisis arrangements would work in practice.
What to review:
1. Business impact analysis and its currency
2. Continuity plans for critical processes, including dependencies
3. Testing — scope, realism and lessons captured
4. Crisis management structure, roles and decision authority
5. Communication plans for staff, customers and regulators
Procedures:
1. Test whether the business impact analysis reflects the current operating model.
2. Review the most recent continuity test for realism — was anything actually switched off?
3. Test whether lessons from previous tests or real incidents were implemented.
4. Assess whether plans account for third-party and technology dependencies.
Red flags:
1. Plans referencing systems or premises no longer used
2. Tests that are desktop discussions only
3. Lessons logged but never actioned
4. Plans assuming staff availability during a regional event
Evidence to request:
1. Business impact analysis
2. Continuity plans
3. Test reports and lessons logs
4. Incident records
Measures:
1. Plans within review cycle
2. Tests performed
3. Lessons implemented

Risk: Liquidity is managed on forecasts that are consistently wrong, so the organisation borrows expensively or is caught short.
Why this matters: Running out of cash kills otherwise profitable businesses. The forecast is what stops that happening.
Audit objective: Assess whether cash forecasting is accurate enough to support liquidity decisions.
What to review:
1. Forecast methodology, horizon and granularity
2. Accuracy of prior forecasts against actual outcomes
3. Inclusion of committed capital, tax and debt service outflows
4. Headroom against facilities and covenant limits
5. Escalation when forecast headroom falls below threshold
Procedures:
1. Compare prior forecasts to actual cash outcomes and quantify the error by horizon.
2. Test whether known commitments were included in forecasts or omitted.
3. Test facility headroom at several dates and whether escalation occurred where policy required.
4. Assess whether business units feed the forecast on a consistent basis.
Red flags:
1. Forecast error consistently in one direction
2. Committed outflows appearing only when they hit
3. Headroom breaches noticed after the fact
4. Forecast prepared by one person with no challenge
Evidence to request:
1. Cash forecasts and actual outcomes
2. Facility agreements and headroom reports
3. Capital commitment schedules
4. Escalation records
Measures:
1. Forecast accuracy by horizon
2. Minimum headroom
3. Escalations raised

Risk: A covenant is breached, or a facility lapses, because compliance is monitored manually and only at reporting dates.
Why this matters: Loan agreements contain promises. Break one and the lender can demand its money back immediately.
Audit objective: Confirm borrowing arrangements are tracked and covenant compliance is monitored continuously.
What to review:
1. Inventory of facilities, maturities and renewal timelines
2. Covenant definitions and how they are calculated
3. Frequency of covenant monitoring versus testing dates
4. Headroom trend and forecast covenant compliance
5. Reporting obligations to lenders and their timeliness
Procedures:
1. Recompute covenants from the lender definitions rather than from management's summary; definitions often differ from statutory measures.
2. Test covenant headroom at each test date and on a forecast basis.
3. Test that lender reporting obligations were met within the required timeframe.
4. Review maturity profile and refinancing plans for concentration risk.
Red flags:
1. Covenants calculated using management-adjusted figures
2. Headroom thin and narrowing without escalation
3. Lender reporting submitted late
4. Facilities maturing within twelve months with no refinancing plan
Evidence to request:
1. Facility and loan agreements
2. Covenant calculations
3. Lender reporting submissions
4. Maturity profile
Measures:
1. Covenant headroom
2. Lender reports on time
3. Debt maturing within 12 months

Sub-process: Foreign Exchange and Interest Rate Risk
Risk: Exposures are hedged on incomplete data or not at all, so earnings swing on market movements the organisation never chose to take.
Why this matters: Currency and interest rate moves can swing profit even when the business is performing exactly as planned.
Audit objective: Assess whether market risk exposures are identified, measured and managed within policy.
What to review:
1. Completeness of exposure identification from the business
2. Hedging policy, ratios and permitted instruments
3. Effectiveness of hedges and any hedge accounting applied
4. Speculative positions and policy breaches
5. Counterparty exposure and credit limits
Procedures:
1. Reconcile hedged exposures to underlying business exposures and quantify unhedged or over-hedged positions.
2. Test compliance with the hedging policy ratio at several dates.
3. Test that instruments used are on the permitted list and that no speculative positions exist.
4. Test hedge effectiveness documentation where hedge accounting is applied.
Red flags:
1. Over-hedging, which is speculation by another name
2. Exposures identified only from the ledger, missing forecast transactions
3. Instruments used outside the approved list
4. Effectiveness testing prepared retrospectively
Evidence to request:
1. Exposure reports and forecasts
2. Hedging policy
3. Deal confirmations and positions
4. Hedge documentation
Measures:
1. Hedge ratio vs. policy
2. Unhedged exposure
3. Policy breaches

Risk: Surplus cash is placed with counterparties or in instruments outside policy, risking capital for marginal yield.
Why this matters: Chasing slightly better returns with spare cash is how companies lose money they were not trying to risk.
Audit objective: Confirm investments comply with policy on instrument, counterparty and tenor.
What to review:
1. Approved instrument and counterparty lists with credit limits
2. Concentration by counterparty and rating
3. Tenor and liquidity of investments against cash needs
4. Valuation and income recognition
5. Authorisation of placements and rollovers
Procedures:
1. Test each investment held against the approved instrument and counterparty list and applicable limits.
2. Analyse concentration by counterparty and rating band against policy.
3. Test authorisation for placements and rollovers, including who can instruct the bank.
4. Agree valuations and accrued income to independent confirmations.
Red flags:
1. Yield chasing into unapproved instruments
2. Concentration with one counterparty above limit
3. Rollovers executed without fresh authorisation
4. Valuations sourced from the counterparty alone
Evidence to request:
1. Investment register and policy
2. Counterparty credit ratings
3. Deal confirmations
4. Bank and custodian statements
Measures:
1. Investments outside policy
2. Counterparty concentration
3. Average tenor vs. need

Risk: Funds move between group entities without documentation, creating tax exposure, regulatory breach and balances nobody can reconcile.
Why this matters: Money moved between group companies without proper agreements creates tax and legal problems later.
Audit objective: Confirm intragroup funding is documented, priced and permitted in each jurisdiction.
What to review:
1. Loan agreements and documentation for intragroup funding
2. Interest pricing and transfer pricing compliance
3. Cash pooling arrangements and participant agreements
4. Regulatory restrictions on cross-border movement and repatriation
5. Reconciliation of intercompany balances
Procedures:
1. Test that intragroup funding has executed agreements and that interest is charged and paid per those terms.
2. Test transfer pricing documentation supporting intragroup interest rates.
3. Reconcile pooling balances between participants and the header account.
4. Test compliance with local restrictions on capital movement for a sample of jurisdictions.
Red flags:
1. Funding advanced with no agreement
2. Interest accrued but never settled
3. Pool balances unreconciled between entities
4. Repatriation executed without checking local rules
Evidence to request:
1. Intercompany loan agreements
2. Transfer pricing documentation
3. Cash pool statements
4. Local regulatory advice
Measures:
1. Funding with agreements
2. Intercompany reconciling differences
3. Interest settled vs. accrued

Sub-process: Guarantees, Letters of Credit and Off-Balance Sheet Commitments
Risk: Guarantees and contingent commitments are given and forgotten, so the organisation carries obligations that appear nowhere in its reporting.
Why this matters: Guarantees are promises to pay if someone else does not. They are easy to give and easy to forget.
Audit objective: Confirm contingent obligations are authorised, recorded, monitored and disclosed.
What to review:
1. Register of guarantees, letters of credit, bonds and indemnities
2. Authorisation and who may commit the organisation
3. Expiry monitoring and release of expired instruments
4. Fees paid on unused or expired facilities
5. Disclosure of contingent liabilities
Procedures:
1. Obtain confirmations from banks of all instruments outstanding and reconcile to the internal register.
2. Test authorisation for instruments issued in the period.
3. Identify expired instruments still incurring fees and test whether release was pursued.
4. Reconcile the register to contingent liability disclosure.
Red flags:
1. Bank confirmations revealing instruments not on the register
2. Guarantees issued by subsidiaries without group approval
3. Fees paid on instruments no longer needed
4. Contingent liabilities disclosed only in round terms
Evidence to request:
1. Guarantee and instrument register
2. Bank confirmations
3. Board and delegated authorities
4. Contingent liability disclosures
Measures:
1. Instruments not on register
2. Expired instruments still live
3. Fees on unused facilities

Sub-process: Treasury System Access and Dealing Controls
Risk: A single treasury user can create, confirm and settle a deal, allowing funds to be moved with no independent check.
Why this matters: If the same person can do a deal and settle it, money can move with no independent check at all.
Audit objective: Confirm dealing, confirmation and settlement are segregated and that treasury system access reflects that.
What to review:
1. Segregation between front, middle and back office
2. System roles and conflicting access combinations
3. Independent confirmation of deals with counterparties
4. Standing settlement instructions and their amendment
5. Dealer mandates, limits and recorded lines
Procedures:
1. Map treasury system roles against a segregation matrix and test for users able to deal and settle.
2. Test independent confirmation of a sample of deals directly with counterparties.
3. Test amendments to standing settlement instructions for independent verification.
4. Test dealer authority against mandates for a sample of transactions.
Red flags:
1. Dealers able to amend settlement instructions
2. Confirmations returned to the dealer rather than the back office
3. Standing instructions changed without verification
4. Deals executed outside recorded lines
Evidence to request:
1. Treasury system user and role listings
2. Deal confirmations
3. Standing settlement instruction change logs
4. Dealer mandates
Measures:
1. Dealing/settlement conflicts
2. Deals independently confirmed
3. SSI changes verified

Sub-process: Bank Account Governance and Fee Analysis
Risk: Bank accounts exist outside treasury's knowledge and banking fees are paid without review, wasting money and creating fraud exposure.
Why this matters: Companies routinely have bank accounts nobody at head office knows about.
Audit objective: Confirm the organisation knows every bank account it holds and pays only the fees it agreed.
What to review:
1. Completeness of the bank account inventory
2. Account opening and closing authority
3. Dormant accounts and their closure
4. Bank fee schedules versus fees charged
5. Bank service quality and rationalisation opportunities
Procedures:
1. Obtain confirmations directly from all banking relationships and reconcile to the internal account inventory.
2. Test account opening and closing authorisation for the period.
3. Identify dormant accounts and test why they remain open.
4. Recompute a sample of bank charges against the agreed fee schedule.
Red flags:
1. Accounts confirmed by banks that treasury did not know about
2. Accounts opened by local management
3. Dormant accounts retained "just in case"
4. Fees charged above the agreed tariff
Evidence to request:
1. Bank confirmations
2. Internal account inventory
3. Account opening authorisations
4. Fee schedules and bank statements
Measures:
1. Accounts not in inventory
2. Dormant accounts open
3. Fee overcharges recovered
